### Overview
This model is designed to investigate how thymic stromal stiffness influences thymocyte (immature T-cells present in the thymus) migration, T-cell receptor (TCR) signaling and ultimately cell fate during thymic selection. Rather than treating thymic selection as a static threshold problem, the model represents selection as an emergent property arising from the interaction between spatial migration, mechanical adaptation, TCR-pMHC binding kinetics, and intracellular signal accumulation. The model combines:

1. **An Agent-Based Model (ABM)** representing spatial migration of individual thymocytes through a heterogeneous thymic environment and interactions with stromal cells.
2. **Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs)** representing intracellular cytoskeletal priming and cumulative TCR signaling.
3. **A kinetic proofreading framework** based on the work of McKeithan and subsequent work by Altan-Bonnet & Germain. This replaces arbitrary signaling thresholds with mechanistically derived signaling probabilities.

The central hypothesis of this model is that thymic stromal properties (primarily, stiffness) influence T-cell selection through two coupled mechanisms:

1. Direct modulation of TCR signaling through force-dependent effects on TCR functioning (such as catch-bond kinetics modulation and nanoclustering) and cytoskeletal priming (concept of the cytoskeleton and associated signaling pathways of cells which have migrated through stiffer substrates being in different states than those of cells which migrated through softer substrates);
2. Indirect modulation of contact dynamics with antigen-presenting stromal cells though modulation of thymocyte migration (which affects how much the thymocytes come in contact with stromal cells).
The mechanical state modulates the efficiency and organization of TCR signal transduction rather than acting solely as a positive amplifier. Depending on cytoskeletal architecture and activation state, mechanical organization may facilitate force transmission, receptor clustering and signal propagation, or constrain receptor mobility and promote inhibitory regulation. The present model represents only the net signal-enhancing branch of this relationship.

Rather than modifying selection thresholds arbitrarily, stromal stiffness alters the probability of productive signaling events through established mechanobiological and kinetic proofreading principles, allowing thymocyte fate to emerge naturally from the interaction between spatial migration, mechanical adaptation and intracellular signaling. This model is intended as a hypothesis-generating framework (an eg.: A biphasic relationship exists between stromal stiffness and the stringency of negative selection), rather than a predictive digital twin of the thymus. It integrates experimentally established mechanisms of TCR kinetic proofreading, force-dependent TCR–pMHC interactions and cell migration with phenomenological representations of cytoskeletal memory and mechanotransduction where quantitative thymocyte-specific data are currently lacking. Predictions should therefore be interpreted as mechanistic hypotheses whose robustness is evaluated through sensitivity analyses and whose validity ultimately requires experimental testing. Looking a bit ahead of these limitations, this model can act as a platform that promotes the integration of mechanobiology and immunology (recently, ‘mechano-immunology’ has started to be used for this combination) which generates fresh perspectives to address long-term problems of auto-immunity, immunological deficiencies and cancer.

### Why ABM was chosen for this simulation.

### Rules of this model

**1. Spatial Agent-Based Model**

The thymus is represented as a two-dimensional grid consisting of a cortical region and a medullary region. In a healthy young thymus, the cortex is larger and more densely cellular than the medulla, but the exact cortex-to-medulla volume ratio varies by species, age, and measurement method. Additionally, while histology and pathology references consistently show cortex predominance in normal thymus, age-related involution reduces cortical mass and blurs the corticomedullary boundary. Due to these uncertainties in current literature, the cortex and medulla are considered to be of same size with the thymocytes being introduced at the top of the cortex. Each grid cell has a side of 10 μm and each node possesses:
- local substrate stiffness;
- occupancy status of a stromal cell (representing thymic epithelial cells/TECs and other antigen presenting cells/APCs like dendritic cells).

Instead of assuming homogeneous regions, stiffness is spatially heterogeneous. Spatial correlation is introduced using smoothed random fields rather than completely random values, producing biologically plausible stiffness patches. As there is currently no convincing quantitative evidence that the cortex is consistently softer or stiffer than the medulla, for this simulation (focused on the mechanical properties of the stroma), three situations will be tested:
1.  [Null hypothesis] The entire thymic stroma is considered as a mechanically uniform region with stiffness of 1-3 kPa (based on the work from David Mooney’s lab):
2.  The cortex is stiffer than the medulla;
3.  The medulla is stiffer than the cortex.

Instead of a single stiffness architecture, this three-scenario approach is chosen due to its potential of turning an uncertain biological fact into a falsifiable modelling question. If any of these scenarios produce an absurd result (for eg., almost all the cells die through negative selection) then this might suggest specific things about the thymic stroma that can be experimentally validated in the future. More importantly, since the purpose of this simulation is to investigate how stromal stiffness affects thymic selection, other stiffness ranges will be tested as well. Some of these ranges will be inspired by existing studies that present different values than the one mentioned above (such as the study by which shows that the stiffness range is 6-12 kPa). Furthermore, the effects of fibrosis and involution-associated stromal changes will be probed as well by setting the range to their corresponding stiffness values.  

Regarding the occupancy status of these grid points, since the current literature does not contain any explicit data regarding cell densities of different thymic regions but mentions the quantitative dominance of thymocytes compared to non-thymocytes, only 1% of the grid points will contain stromal cells in this model (which is a subject to sensitivity analysis). For the sake of simplicity in this model, these stromal cells are not separated into more specific identities (such as cTECs, mTECs, dendritic cells, etc.) and each of these cells have the same level of pMHC expression without introducing the distinction between MHC class I and MHC class II complexes.

The duration of a single time step was chosen to be 1 min in consideration of the following points:
- With the agent speed having a maximum value of 25 μm/min (more on this in the cell migration section), cells should not "teleport" unrealistically (for eg., if the time step is chosen to be 10 mins, a thymocyte can migrate 150 μm which is equal to 15 grid points, resulting in unnatural behavior);  
- Signaling should change smoothly;
- Simulation should remain computationally tractable.

---

**2. Agent properties**

Each agent (which represent the thymocytes) possesses permanent and dynamic properties.

**Permanent properties:** Assigned once at initialization and will include:

·        **Cell size:** As the diameter of thymocytes vary greatly between different developmental stages (from 6-7 μm of double positive/DP thymocytes upto 12 μm of earlier double negative stages/DN), 10 μm is chosen for simplicity.  

·        **Intrinsic TCR off-rate:** Each thymocyte receives a base dissociation rate **(**![](data:image/png;base64,)sampled from a biological distribution (preferably log-normal because dissociation rates are strictly positive and the binding kinetic parameters often span orders of magnitude and are approximately log-normal rather than normally distributed), representing diversity of the TCR repertoire. This replaces arbitrary affinity assignment. There is however, no published distribution of koff ​ across all thymocytes, because each thymocyte expresses a unique TCR and its dissociation kinetics depend on the specific peptide–MHC it encounters. Instead, what exists are libraries of experimentally measured TCR–pMHC kinetics (using surface plasmon resonance (SPR), bio-membrane force probe (BFP), optical tweezers, micropipette adhesion assays). Classic datasets come from the work of Brian McKeithan, Johannes Huppa, Michael Dustin, and Cheng Zhu. These studies report many individual ![](data:image/png;base64,)values for different TCR–pMHC pairs rather than a population distribution, and the following steps will be done to assign ![](data:image/png;base64,) to each thymocyte:
- Compile published ![](data:image/png;base64,) values.
- Fit a probability distribution to those values.
- Sample one value per thymocyte (or clone).

==**Signaling protein expression:**== Each thymocyte independently samples relative expression levels of ZAP70 (ZAP70i) from experimentally established datasets (like the Human Protein Atlas). This modifies signaling competence through

![](data:image/png;base64,)

creating natural cell-to-cell variability. ZAP70 is chosen for this simulation due to recent studies suggesting that its expression acts as the bottleneck for the TCR signaling pathway.

**Dynamic properties** (updated every timestep): Each thymocyte stores:
- Position in the spatial grid;
- Age (T<sub>res</sub>, which is time elapsed since that thymocyte was introduced);
- Cytoskeletal priming or C(t);
- Mechanotransduction pathway priming or M(t);
- Cumulative TCR signal or X(t).

---

**4. Migration**

For actual thymocytes, the type and speed of migration have been observed to vary through different stages. Cortical DP thymocytes generally move slowly (~3–8 μm/min) in a random-walk fashion, while positively selected thymocytes are much faster (~10–15 μm/min or even higher in some studies) and show biased migration toward the medulla. Cells undergoing negative selection can become highly confined and slow down dramatically. This creates an interpretation problem: Do cells speed up because they are in the medulla or are they faster because they have been positively selected? While this has not been completely answered, current evidence seems to be leaning towards the latter.

For this simulation, the focus is on the effects of the substrate/regional stiffness upon thymocyte migration with the relationship between speed and developmental stage (and cytokine gradients as well) being kept for a more advanced future version. Therefore, thymocyte movement is governed by two components:

1. **Directional bias toward the medulla**: Implemented as a simple probability (p<sub>bias</sub>) favoring movement toward the medulla without explicitly modelling chemokine diffusion. This is actually a model parameter set to 0.5 (not something measured directly) and represents the probability that a thymocyte follows the net chemotactic cue toward the medulla rather than executing an unbiased exploratory move.
2. **Local stiffness-dependent migration probability:** Migration follows v(S) ==defined by==

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Where,

Vmax is the upper limit of thymocyte migration speed that has been observed under physiological conditions using intravital two-photon imaging studies. Based on two-photon imaging studies which have reported upper thymocyte migration speeds to sometimes exceed 25 μm/min under physiological conditions, vmax is set to 25 μm/min,

Klow and Khigh are stiffness values where speed rises to half‑maximum and falls to half‑maximum, respectively,

nlow and nhigh are the hill coefficients which control the steepness of the transition from low to high stiffness.

This term v(S) is connected to a thymocyte’s probability of moving and how far it will move in a timestep.

The equation for v(S) is a product of a rising Hill term and a falling Hill term creates a peak at intermediate stiffness. This is not derived from a specific mechanical equation of motion, but is a phenomenological envelope function that captures the experimentally observed biphasic dependence of cell speed on substrate stiffness. Rather than a monotonic response, this equation produces a biphasic relation between substrate stiffness and cell migration speed:
- slow movement on very soft substrates (lower probability of moving and shorter distance migrated in a time-step);
- maximal movement at intermediate stiffness (higher probability of moving and larger distance migrated in a time-step);
- reduced movement on excessively stiff substrates (same as very soft substrate conditions).

Because migration is simulated explicitly, this equation does not directly contribute to TCR signaling, but influences how the contact probability and duration of a thymocyte with a stromal cell. Due to the simulation biphasic nature of migration, interesting unforeseen outcomes can emerge such as a thymocyte in intermediate stiffness regions might be expected to migrate more and interact with higher number of stromal cells and hence, have higher TCR signaling compared to a thymocyte on very soft or stiff substrates. However, this might not be the case as the thymocyte in either of the latter situations might interact with one/few stromal cells for a longer duration, thus accumulating a higher TCR signal (and of course, other factors like simulated noise and cytoskeletal priming would also have to be kept in mind).

**6. Cytoskeletal priming ODE**

Mechanical history of the substrate that a thymocytes has migrated on is represented through a dimensionless cytoskeletal priming state C(t) (with value between 0 and 1) rather than instantaneous stiffness. The governing equation is:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Where, kc is an ODE rate constant and determines how rapidly does the cytoskeletal network adapts to the current stiffness.

And,

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Where KC  is the stiffness value where the priming state of the cytoskeletal network is half of the maximum.

This term Ceq represents gradual adaptation of the actomyosin cytoskeleton to local substrate stiffness and stores recent mechanical history, evolving continuously as the thymocyte migrates through regions of different stiffness. At every substrate stiffness there is an equilibrium level of cytoskeletal organization arising through processes such as actin polymerization/depolymerization, myosin recruitment/turnover, crosslink formation/breakdown, cortical tension adaptation,, and the cell relaxes toward it with rate kC. This equation is essentially the standard relaxation equation used throughout systems biology and has been used for receptor adaptation, transcriptional adaptation, YAP/TAZ mechanosensing and focal adhesion maturation.

**7. Mechanotransduction priming ODE**

Mechanosensitive competence is represented independently as M(t) following

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Where, kM (similar to kC) represents how quickly downstream mechanosensitive pathways respond to changes in cytoskeletal state and move towards a steady state represented by

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Where KM  is the stiffness value where the strength of the mechanosensitive signal is half of the maximum.

This specific priming module was inspired from a 2018 paper (titled “_Cutting Edge: Piezo1 Mechanosensors Optimize Human T Cell Activation_”) was really the first direct demonstration that Piezo1 is not merely involved in migration or development—it actively enhances TCR signalling. The authors showed that:

- Piezo1 deficiency attenuated downstream TCR signalling,
- a Piezo1 agonist could rescue activation even under otherwise suboptimal mechanical stimulation,
- Piezo1-mediated Ca²⁺ influx activates calpain,
- calpain reorganizes the cortical actin scaffold,
- overall T-cell activation is enhanced.

Furthermore, the 2026 Frontiers review by reinforces this, describing Piezo1 as a hub that converts membrane tension, substrate stiffness, and synaptic force into Ca²⁺ influx, NFAT activation, and cytokine production. However, this variable represents integrated YAP/TAZ, Piezo1 and Integrin survival signalling.

The equation is a linear Hill equation which limits the value of α between 1 (when C is 0, representing a ‘no-primed cytoskeletal network’ state) and 1 + αmax (when C is 1, representing the ‘fully-primed or saturated’ state). This parameter α connects substrate stiffness and cytoskeletal state with the strength of TCR signalling. _[α(C) represents the efficiency with which a successfully proofread TCR signal is assembled into a productive actin-supported LAT signalosome and propagated through the canonical proximal TCR signalling network, represents the integrated mechanotransductional state of the thymocyte arising from mechanosensitive signalling pathways that are treated separately from cytoskeletal force transmission. Although these pathways interact with the cytoskeleton biologically, they are represented as a distinct coarse-grained state variable to avoid conflating structural mechanical adaptation with downstream mechanotransducive signalling.]_

**9. Force generation**

Recently, a new perspective of considering the TCR as a mechanosensor has been gaining experimental support and this part of the model is derived from that perspective. Local stiffness influences how well a TCR can sense and transmit force applied on it by modulating its dynamics (including immunological synapse formation and TCR nanoclustering) with cytoskeleton organisation acting as the mediator. This relationship between substrate stiffness and TCR dynamics is encapsulated by the term F(S):

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Where KF  is the stiffness value where the force transmitted by TCR is half of the maximum and Fmax is the maximum force that can be transmitted. While this equation directly maps substrate stiffness (kPa) to force (pN). This is a phenomenological simplification as in reality, force transmission depends on cell spreading area and adhesion site density.

In addition to the TCR transmitting the applied force, state of the cytoskeletal priming is also crucial in determining the extent of the force transmitted to the thymocyte’s intracellular networks. So, this force transmission efficiency (Feff) is composed of two parts:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Where β is the gain coefficient which dictates how strongly the mechanical input amplifies the intracellular force transmission and whose value will range from 0 to 1 (this will be subjected to sensitivity analysis). This equation structure is commonly used in phenomenological modelling systems for ensuring that if there is no mechanical stimulus (C = 0), the mathematical multiplier reduces exactly to 1, meaning the pathway preserves its baseline (= F(S)) levels rather than dropping to zero.

This “cytoskeleton-mediated modulation of TCR force transmission” model is analogous to the “Inside-out signalling” used to describe Integrin function. In this model, substrate stiffness is considered to influence both TCR dynamics (allowing previously experienced stiffness to influence future TCR-pMHC interactions) and TCR force transmission to the downstream pathways.

---

**10. Catch-slip bond kinetics**

TCR-pMHC binding dynamics have been observed to follow the established two-pathway catch-slip model. This implies that as a catch bond in certain regimes, the lifetime _increases_ under tensile force, up to a point. The implication is that the effective dwell time, and therefore the signal a thymocyte accumulates, is not determined by affinity alone. It is determined by affinity under a particular mechanical load, which depends on cytoskeletal tension, which depends on substrate stiffness. An important disclaimer is that a single TCR-pMHC bond strength is most likely dominated by biochemical factors and is not mechanically modulated significantly. However, in this simulation, all the TCRs of a single thymocyte and pMHC of stromal cells are bundled into a single term and this introduces additional processes like TCR nanoclustering into the TCR-pMHC bond kinetics.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Where, ![](data:image/png;base64,) is the dissociation rate of the catch pathway at zero force (s⁻¹).

![](data:image/png;base64,) is a characteristic force that quantifies how strongly the catch pathway is stabilised by force (lower ![](data:image/png;base64,) → more sensitive).

![](data:image/png;base64,) is the dissociation rate of the slip pathway at zero force (s⁻¹).

![](data:image/png;base64,) is the characteristic force for slip‑induced dissociation (lower ![](data:image/png;base64,) → faster slip at moderate forces).

This formulation originates from transition-state theory and Kramers-like force-dependent barrier crossing. It captures the idea that force can either stabilize one dissociation pathway or accelerate another, producing a nonmonotonic lifetime curve with a force-optimal regime. The exponential terms are Boltzmann factors: ![](data:image/png;base64,) translated into force‑dependent barrier heights. The catch pathway has a negative sign in the exponent because increasing force raises the effective barrier height (stabilizes the bound state up to a point). The slip pathway has a positive sign because force always lowers its barrier, accelerating dissociation. For TCR–pMHC, this framework is supported by agonist catch-bond measurements (This was shown explicitly for TCR–pMHC interactions by the Zhu and Chen labs). This term, G(Feff), which allows substrate stiffness to modulate TCR-pMHC bond kinetics is combined with the base dissociation rate of each thymocyte to maintain biological diversity. Therefore, the final equation is:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Each thymocyte, therefore, combines intrinsic repertoire diversity (![](data:image/png;base64,)) with dynamic mechanical modulation (G(Feff)). If the thymocyte does not experience any mechanical force, Feff becomes 0, which makes G(Feff) = 1 and hence![](data:image/png;base64,)

**10. Kinetic proofreading**

Rather than using arbitrary signaling thresholds, productive signaling is determined through the McKeithan kinetic proofreading model (published in 1995, this model presents a system of ODEs describing the kinetics of sequential TCR complex modification) that provides an established framework to convert biochemical ligand binding to signal magnitude.

The probability that a productive signalling event is completed downstream of TCR-pMHC binding is KP(Feff), described by the equation:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Where,

N is the number of proofreading steps (The number of sequential biochemical modifications (typically phosphorylations) that must occur before the TCR engagement produces a stable downstream signal. If the cascade resets before reaching step N, no signal is generated) and is kept at N = 7 for this simulation (based on the work of Altan-Bonnet & Germain, 2005).

kSHP1 is the rate which SHP-1 (a phosphatase) de-phosphorylates crucial signaling sites and prevents the signal from travelling further downstream. Its value is taken to be 1 s<sup>-1</sup> from the work of Altan-Bonnet & Germain, 2005.

Consequently, changes in

- Effective force (which combines both substrate stiffness and cytoskeletal priming);
- TCR repertoire;
- signaling protein expression.

all alter productive signaling through established biochemical mechanisms.

---

**11. Threshold calculation**

Selection thresholds are not chosen arbitrarily. Instead, published TCR-pMHC kinetic proofreading parameters and experimentally observed TCR off-rate distributions are used to estimate productive signalling probabilities. _As this initial proof-of-concept model does not distinguish between MHC class I and class II, or between CD4 and CD8 lineages, threshold calibration was performed using published data from the well-characterised OT-I TCR system (H-2Kb-restricted). This provides a consistent set of ligands with known selection outcomes and measured binding kinetics. Future extensions of the model will incorporate lineage-specific distinctions as additional data become available._

Selection thresholds are then defined from these distributions rather than assigned manually in through the following steps which provides the model with mechanistic interpretation and scientific testability:

·        Take published koff estimates for pMHC interactions (mainly derived using SPR-based experiments) at each selection boundary;

·        Compute relative signal output using the kinetic proofreading formula;

·        Normalise these to the scale of your simulation's cumulative signal variable;

·        Set thresholds at those normalised values.

_The thresholds derived from these k_off values are phenomenological decision boundaries, not directly measured biological constants. They provide a consistent scale for interpreting simulation outputs under different mechanical conditions._ The selection thresholds represent biochemical decision boundaries — the minimum signal required for survival and the maximum signal compatible with positive rather than negative selection. These boundaries are properties of the downstream signalling machinery (primarily apoptosis associated processes), not of the mechanical environment. The mechanical model's job is then to ask: given these fixed biochemical boundaries, does cytoskeletal state help or hinder a cell in crossing them?

---

**12. Selection outcomes**

After residence time expires:

·        Death by neglect: Occurs when TCR signaling remains below the neglect threshold.

·        Positive selection: Cells with intermediate cumulative signaling survive positive selection.

Negative selection occurs immediately if cumulative productive signaling exceeds the deletion threshold and the cell is removed. Lineage commitment (CD4/CD8/T<sub>reg</sub>) is intentionally omitted from the first prototype and can be incorporated later by including MHC class distinction and downstream transcriptional modules (e.g. ThPOK/Runx3 dynamics) rather than simple signal thresholds.

---

**13. TCR signaling ODE**

Cumulative TCR signaling combines the term for contact formation, cytoskeletal priming and probability of a productive signaling event and evolves according to:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Where, λ is the signal decay rate which is set to 0.02 min-1. According to this equation, the signal production depends on

- Presence or absence of contact with a stromal cell (if E(t) = 0, then the signal does not grow but gradually decreases when contact is lost);
- Cytoskeletal amplification (if one thymocyte has migrated through stiffer substrates than another one, its cytoskeletal networks are considered to be in specific states which allow greater force transmission and signal accumulation);
- Successful proofreading (for each thymocyte this depends on its expression levels of signalling proteins and how strongly its TCR binds to pMHC which is influenced by the substrate stiffness through the cytoskeletal organisation modulating TCR’s catch-bond kinetics and receptor dynamics).

**14. Residence time**

==Each thymocyte possesses an individual residence time== Tres sampled from an experimentally motivated distribution. Data from BrdU-pulse chase experiments, RAG-GFP molecular timer experiments and Intravital two-photon imaging (the most suitable one or a combination if the data is compatible among these experiments) will be obtained and fitted to either a gamma or log normal distribution. Age increases continuously during migration. When age = Tres the cell exits the selection environment and its fate is evaluated.

Negative selection is evaluated continuously throughout the simulation and immediately removes cells whose cumulative signal exceeds the deletion threshold.

---

**15. Outputs**

The simulation produces

- spatial maps of thymocyte migration,
- stiffness heatmaps,
- trajectories of individual cells,
- distributions of cumulative TCR signaling,
- cytoskeletal priming dynamics,
- selection outcome tables,
- percentages of

- negative selection,
- death by neglect,
- positive selection,

- parameter sensitivity analyses.

### Limitations of this model and possible future modifications

·        3D grid and inclusion of other mechanical properties such as fibre orientation and ECM composition, MHCI/II distinction, cytokine fields, CD4/CD8 commitment elaboration through ThPOK and Runx activity, competition for stromal contacts and crowding-dependent mechanotransduction, cell proliferation and how it affects signalling dynamics such as cytoskeletal priming, dynamic ECM and how different cell types reshape the microenvironment, Relationship between speed, developmental stage and cytokine gradients, Further addition of factors contributing to biological noise (like varying expression levels of different signalling proteins), Effects of changing stromal properties upon stromal cell densities, slowing of cells upon interaction with APCs (and the amount varies between cells that were then observed to be positively or negatively selected)

·        **Mechanotransduction survival module:** Main reasons for excluding it from the first version: lack of sufficient data which connects mechanosensitive survival pathways to changing selection outcomes and lack of an established framework like the kinetic proof-reading that allows determination of non-arbitrary survival thresholds.

·        Future extensions of the model will refine the thresholds using additional data (e.g., Nur77-GFP reporter studies, lineage-specific calibrations) as they become available and as the model is extended to include MHC-I/II and CD4/8 distinctions.

Piezo1 is part of a conserved class of mechanically activated ion channels across eukaryote species, non-selectively permeable to cations, with a slight preference for Ca2+ ions [[113](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4409/9/2/364#B113-cells-09-00364),[114](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4409/9/2/364#B114-cells-09-00364)].
- Biophysical {Aspects} of {T} {Lymphocyte} {Activation} at the {Immune} {Synapse}: Moreover, it has been shown that the integrin bonds “remember” the history of the forces they have been submitted to. This phenomenon was called “cyclic mechanical reinforcement,” as the bond strength accumulates over repeated cycles of forces and is maintained after force removal (65). For instance, fibronectin/α5β1 integrin bonds dissociate within 1 s at a force of 5 pN, while upon cyclic mechanical reinforcement, the bond lifetimes can be extended to 14 s. Similar mechanisms apply to LFA-1/ICAM-1-specific bonds
